transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Welcome to Launch Window, I'm Hannah Wright. Today we're talking money and rockets with space investor Raj Mehta and aerospace engineer Olivia Grant.

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: Thanks Hannah, excited to be here.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: How big is the space business right now?

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: The global space economy is around $570 billion a year, and most of that is commercial, not government.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: What changed to make it so commercial?

transcript.speaker: Olivia
transcript.text: Reusability. SpaceX landed its first orbital-class Falcon 9 booster back in December 2015, and that rewrote launch economics.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And the Moon is back in fashion.

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: It is, but it's still an exclusive club. Only the US, Russia and China have ever landed on the Moon.

transcript.speaker: Olivia
transcript.text: The commercial landers are where it gets interesting for me. That's where the risk-taking is.

transcript.speaker: Olivia
transcript.text: People forget that the International Space Station has had humans on board continuously since November 2000.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Raj, what's it like raising money for space startups?

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: When we pitched our first satellite startup in 2019, three investors literally laughed us out of the room. Now those same firms call us.

transcript.speaker: Olivia
transcript.text: Starship will land astronauts on the Moon by 2026.

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: I'm more cautious. I think regulation will be the real bottleneck, not the hardware.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Raj, Olivia, thank you both for joining Launch Window.
